<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite sparse systematic evidence, current exercise heat safety recommendations suggest that antihistamines blunt sweating and increase the risk for heat-related injury during exertional heat stress. The primary purpose of the present study was to examine whether diphenhydramine hydrochloride (DPH), a first-generation antihistamine, affects the sweating, core temperature, and heart rate (HR) response during exertional heat stress using a double-blind randomized crossover design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      On two occasions separated by >48 h, 20 healthy adults (10 females, 23 ± 3 yr, body surface area: 1.9 ± 0.2 m
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      , body mass index: 23.7 ± 2.2 kg·m
                      <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                      ) orally consumed either 50 mg of DPH or placebo (PLA), and then rested for 2 h in a climate-controlled room maintained at 30°C and 35% relative humidity (heat index of ~29°C), followed by a 60-min fixed-heat production treadmill walk (6.3 ± 1.0 W·kg
                      <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                      ). Whole-body sweat loss, local sweat rate, rectal temperature (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">T</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>rec</jats:sub>
                      ), and HR were measured.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Whole-body sweat loss was not different between conditions (PLA: 406 ± 78 g, DPH: 396 ± 75 g;
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.26, treatment effect: −10 g; 95% confidence interval, −28 to 8). No differences were observed for the onset of sweating (PLA: 13.5 ± 2.4 min, DPH: 13.3 ± 2.7 min;
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.79) and steady-state local sweat rate (PLA: 0.83 ± 0.26 mg·cm
                      <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                      ·min
                      <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                      , DPH: 0.82 ± 0.27 mg·cm
                      <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                      ·min
                      <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                      ;
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.99). No difference in baseline
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">T</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>rec</jats:sub>
                      was observed (PLA: 37.09°C ± 0.35°C, DPH: 37.13°C ± 0.33°C;
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.68), and the 60-min Δ
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">T</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>rec</jats:sub>
                      was not different (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.99) between PLA (0.83°C ± 0.29°C) and DPH (0.81°C ± 0.30°C). HR was similar at baseline (PLA: 86 ± 13 bpm, DPH: 84 ± 11 bpm;
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.30) and end-exercise (PLA: 134 ± 28 bpm, DPH: 132 ± 26 bpm;
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.90).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fifty milligrams of DPH does not modify the sweating, core temperature, and HR response during exertional heat stress in young healthy adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Thermal and Cardiovascular Responses during Exertional Heat Stress after Diphenhydramine Use: A Randomized Crossover Trial
